l: freezing of the water, The Sea Fairies, [Illustration: _Chap. 18._
s: Zog's magic freezes all the water in the room while the group sleeps, leaving them trapped inside solid ice with only small air spaces. Queen Aquareine melts the ice and rescues them before they perish.

l: escape from Zog's castle, The Sea Fairies, [Illustration: _Chap. 18._
s: Queen Aquareine leads the escape from Zog's castle after deciding that remaining there is too dangerous. She breaks a window with the golden sword, and the group swims into the vast dome toward its guarded opening.

l: attack on the prince of the sea devils, The Sea Fairies, [Illustration: _Chap. 18._
s: Queen Aquareine plans to attack the prince of the sea devils at the opening in the dome. If she destroys him with the golden sword, the group may swim through the opening into the ocean.

l: The Sea Fairies, The Sea Fairies, [Illustration: _Chap. 19._
s: Zog discovers that Aquareine, Trot, Cap'n Bill, and the Princess are escaping through the broken window and sends wolf-fish after them. Aquareine kills the attackers, but Zog reveals his terrible eel-like form and pursues the four fugitives, destroying her sword and knocking away her wand. King Anko arrives through the dome opening, captures Zog in his coils, and crushes him into lifeless pulp. King Anko then tells the rescued fugitives that they may return home through the dome.

l: Zog, The Sea Fairies, [Illustration: _Chap. 19._
s: Zog sends wolf-fish after the escaping prisoners and then pursues them himself in his concealed monstrous form. He destroys Aquareine's golden sword and sends her fairy wand away, but King Anko captures him in his coils; when Anko releases him, Zog is a lifeless mass of jelly-like pulp.

l: Queen Aquareine, The Sea Fairies, [Illustration: _Chap. 19._
s: Aquareine attacks the wolf-fish with her golden sword, killing them one by one. Zog takes and crushes her sword and then knocks her fairy wand away, leaving her unable to defend the fugitives until King Anko rescues them.

l: King Anko, The Sea Fairies, [Illustration: _Chap. 19._
s: King Anko descends through the dome opening and rescues the fugitives by seizing Zog in his coils. He destroys Zog, then tells the group that they can return home through the dome once his body has cleared the opening.

l: Trot, The Sea Fairies, [Illustration: _Chap. 19._
s: Trot is frightened by the wolf-fish and later sees Zog pursuing the group. When Cap'n Bill believes they will die, she responds that they have done their best and had a fine time.

l: Cap'n Bill, The Sea Fairies, [Illustration: _Chap. 19._
s: Cap'n Bill draws Trot close and prepares to die with her when Zog surrounds the fugitives. After King Anko's arrival, Cap'n Bill is rescued along with the others and follows Anko toward the ocean above.

l: the four explorers, The Sea Fairies, [Illustration: _Chap. 19._
s: Aquareine, Trot, Cap'n Bill, and the Princess escape the castle through a broken window but are attacked by wolf-fish and pursued by Zog. King Anko rescues them, and they follow him through the dome toward home.

l: vast dome, The Sea Fairies, [Illustration: _Chap. 19._
s: The four fugitives try to reach the opening in the dome while fleeing the wolf-fish and Zog. King Anko descends through the opening and later says the way home will be open after he withdraws his body.

l: battle between Zog and King Anko, The Sea Fairies, [Illustration: _Chap. 19._
s: The confrontation ends almost immediately because Zog is surprised and his fear of King Anko destroys his magic power. King Anko coils around Zog and crushes him, leaving no living remnant or recognizable form.

l: King Anko's rescue, The Sea Fairies, [Illustration: _Chap. 19._
s: King Anko's rescue saves Aquareine, Trot, Cap'n Bill, and the Princess from Zog's attack. After defeating Zog, he provides them a safe route through the dome and back home.

l: The Sea Fairies, The Sea Fairies, [Illustration: _Chap. 20._
s: Trot and Cap'n Bill visit King Anko's alabaster palace with Aquareine and Clia after Zog's destruction. Anko explains how he found Zog's castle, tells the story of his third pain, and claims that the law of the ocean gives him ownership of those whose lives he saves. He orders Aquareine and Clia to take Trot and Cap'n Bill home and restore them to their natural forms. Before they leave, he shows them the immense coils of his body beneath the palace.

l: Trot, The Sea Fairies, [Illustration: _Chap. 20._
s: Trot briefly cries from relief after Zog's destruction, then visits King Anko's palace with Cap'n Bill, Aquareine, and Clia. She questions Anko about his third pain and corrects his mistaken versions of names and events. Trot agrees that she is ready to return home, while saying that she has enjoyed the visit and will always love the mermaids.

l: Cap'n Bill, The Sea Fairies, [Illustration: _Chap. 20._
s: Cap'n Bill comforts Trot and hopes to take her home, though he remains with the mermaids and King Anko out of politeness and gratitude. He visits Anko's palace, challenges the king's claim that Captain Kidd was called Captain Kid Glove, and approves of Anko's order to send them home. He is impressed by the enormous size of Anko's body.

l: King Anko, The Sea Fairies, [Illustration: _Chap. 20._
s: King Anko explains that he located Zog's castle through a hole beneath the body of the sea-devil prince and arrived in time to help destroy Zog. He tells Trot about his third pain, which came from swallowing an anchor and chain, and about the mustard poultice used to treat it. Claiming authority under the law of the ocean, he orders that Trot and Cap'n Bill be returned home and restored to their natural forms.

l: Queen Aquareine, The Sea Fairies, [Illustration: _Chap. 20._
s: Aquareine accompanies Trot and Cap'n Bill to King Anko's palace and observes the formal ceremony required there. She explains that the king's dignity must be maintained and later agrees to escort the earth travelers home. She and Clia are pleased when Trot says she will always love the mermaids.

l: Princess Clia, The Sea Fairies, [Illustration: _Chap. 20._
s: Clia accompanies Aquareine, Trot, and Cap'n Bill to King Anko's palace and joins in the ceremony of allegiance. She agrees to escort Trot and Cap'n Bill home and affectionately kisses Trot before their departure.

l: Zog, The Sea Fairies, [Illustration: _Chap. 20._
s: Zog is described as King Anko's enemy for centuries and as the evil genius whose powers threatened Trot, Cap'n Bill, Aquareine, and Clia. He is destroyed after Anko discovers the enchanted castle beneath the sea-devil prince.

l: mermaids, The Sea Fairies, [Illustration: _Chap. 20._
s: The mermaids are described as faithful friends who protected and helped Trot and Cap'n Bill during their dangers. Aquareine and Clia regret only that inviting earth people to visit the ocean exposed them to dangers unsuitable for their nature.

l: Pacific Ocean, The Sea Fairies, [Illustration: _Chap. 20._
s: The ocean is presented as a beautiful home without sunstrokes, mosquitoes, earthquakes, or candy shops, though it is dangerous and unnatural for earth people. Its inhabitants follow a law under which anyone who saves a living creature from violent death owns that creature for life.

l: Anko's palace, The Sea Fairies, [Illustration: _Chap. 20._
s: King Anko's palace is a vast circular structure made entirely of polished alabaster, with a domed roof and round openings instead of doors and windows. Its halls contain engraved scenes of ocean life and woven sea-grass rugs, while the central chamber conceals thousands of coils of Anko's body beneath a purple-and-gold coverlet.

l: the earth, The Sea Fairies, [Illustration: _Chap. 20._
s: The earth is described as the natural home of Trot and Cap'n Bill, whose sea forms are to be changed back when they return. Anko says that the ocean is not a proper dwelling place for earth people because they remain constantly in danger underwater.

l: the law of the ocean, The Sea Fairies, [Illustration: _Chap. 20._
s: The law of the ocean states that whoever saves a living creature from violent death owns that creature forever while life lasts. King Anko invokes this law to claim authority over Trot, Cap'n Bill, Aquareine, and Clia, but uses that authority to order the travelers' return home.

l: the destruction of Zog, The Sea Fairies, [Illustration: _Chap. 20._
s: Zog's destruction ends the chief danger facing Trot, Cap'n Bill, Aquareine, and Clia and removes King Anko's centuries-old enemy. The event also enables the travelers to leave the enchanted castle and return safely to the open sea.

l: the travelers' return home, The Sea Fairies, [Illustration: _Chap. 20._
s: King Anko orders Aquareine and Clia to take Trot and Cap'n Bill home and restore them to their natural forms. Trot is ready to leave, and Cap'n Bill agrees that Anko is correct, although both remain grateful for their experiences and friendships in the ocean.

l: The Sea Fairies, The Sea Fairies, [Illustration: _Chap. 21._
s: Trot, Cap'n Bill, Aquareine, and Princess Clia return to Zog's former castle to see what has become of his slaves before continuing home. Sacho proposes that the former slaves govern themselves under a king, and Cap'n Joe is elected to rule them while Sacho serves as his attendant. The visitors say goodbye to Sacho and Cap'n Joe, then swim through the dome and continue their return journey toward their mermaid home.

l: Trot, The Sea Fairies, [Illustration: _Chap. 21._
s: Trot chooses to return home before going to Giant's Cave and suggests visiting Sacho and the other former slaves. She is pleased that Cap'n Joe has become king and says goodbye before swimming toward home.

l: Cap'n Bill, The Sea Fairies, [Illustration: _Chap. 21._
s: Cap'n Bill agrees to visit the former slaves and says goodbye to his brother, Cap'n Joe. He is relieved that Cap'n Joe is well provided for as king of the castle.

l: Queen Aquareine, The Sea Fairies, [Illustration: _Chap. 21._
s: Aquareine offers to take the travelers back to their mermaid home and leads them past the opening in the dome. She visits the castle to learn the fate of Zog's former slaves and offers Sacho her friendship and assistance.

l: Zog, The Sea Fairies, [Illustration: _Chap. 21._
s: Zog is dead, and his former slaves now inherit his possessions and occupy his castle. His destruction removes the danger from the cavern.

l: Sacho, The Sea Fairies, [Illustration: _Chap. 21._
s: Sacho tells the former slaves that they should remain together, labor for themselves, and choose a ruler. He declines to become king, agrees to serve as Cap'n Joe's attendant and officer, and promises to seek Aquareine's help if necessary.

l: Cap'n Joe, The Sea Fairies, [Illustration: _Chap. 21._
s: Cap'n Joe agrees to rule the former slaves if they want him to and is elected King of the Castle. He tells Cap'n Bill that his new life is easy and peaceful.

l: Zog's slaves, The Sea Fairies, [Illustration: _Chap. 21._
s: Zog's hundreds of former slaves assemble in the golden hall after his death. They decide to remain in the castle, work for their own community, and accept Cap'n Joe as their king.

l: Zog's castle, The Sea Fairies, [Illustration: _Chap. 21._
s: Zog's silver castle is no longer enchanted and becomes the home of his former slaves. The slaves inherit it, continue their work there, and make Cap'n Joe their king.

l: the cavern beneath the sea-devil's rock, The Sea Fairies, [Illustration: _Chap. 21._
s: The cavern is described as safe after Zog's destruction. The travelers reenter it through the opening in the dome and find the castle quiet and peaceful.

l: the destruction of Zog, The Sea Fairies, [Illustration: _Chap. 21._
s: The destruction of Zog ends the danger in the cavern and frees his slaves from his rule. It also leaves the former slaves responsible for governing themselves and managing his possessions.

l: Cap'n Joe's election as king, The Sea Fairies, [Illustration: _Chap. 21._
s: Sacho proposes Cap'n Joe as the ruler because he is no longer occupied with sewing Zog's buttons. The former slaves unanimously accept Cap'n Joe, who is proclaimed King of the Castle.

l: self-government of the former slaves, The Sea Fairies, [Illustration: _Chap. 21._
s: The former slaves decide to remain together and labor for their own benefit rather than for a master. They plan to govern themselves under a ruler chosen from among them, with Sacho helping to maintain order.

l: the return journey home, The Sea Fairies, [Illustration: _Chap. 21._
s: After saying goodbye to Sacho and Cap'n Joe, Trot, Cap'n Bill, Aquareine, and Princess Clia leave the castle. They pass through the opening in the dome and swim through the broad ocean toward their mermaid home.

l: The Sea Fairies, The Sea Fairies, [Illustration: _Chap. 22._
s: Queen Aquareine gives Trot a pearl-set gold ring that will summon the mermaids if she calls “Aquareine” at the ocean’s edge. The mermaids carry Trot and Cap’n Bill across the ocean to the Giant’s Cave, where Princess Clia restores them to their regular shapes. They reunite with their boat, say goodbye to Queen Aquareine and Princess Clia, and leave the cave. Trot and Cap’n Bill are glad to return to their everyday world, though they are pleased to have visited the mermaids.

l: Trot, The Sea Fairies, [Illustration: _Chap. 22._
s: Trot receives a pearl-set gold ring from Queen Aquareine, which will allow her to summon the mermaids for help. She changes back to her usual shape, reunites with Cap’n Bill in their boat, and leaves the Giant’s Cave after saying goodbye to the mermaids.

l: Cap'n Bill, The Sea Fairies, [Illustration: _Chap. 22._
s: Cap’n Bill travels with the mermaids across the ocean and returns to his regular form, including his wooden leg. He helps Trot into their boat and rows them out of the Giant’s Cave, agreeing that the land is best for living while being glad to have seen the mermaids.

l: Queen Aquareine, The Sea Fairies, [Illustration: _Chap. 22._
s: Queen Aquareine gives Trot a valuable pearl-set gold ring and promises to hear her call and assist her if she wears it. She asks Trot to speak well of mermaids when ignorant earth people condemn them, then says goodbye before disappearing beneath the water.

l: Princess Clia, The Sea Fairies, [Illustration: _Chap. 22._
s: Princess Clia guides Trot and Cap’n Bill to the Giant’s Cave and explains that the entrance lies near the bottom of the sea. She changes them back to their regular shapes and helps them return to their boat before saying goodbye.

l: mermaids, The Sea Fairies, [Illustration: _Chap. 22._
s: The mermaids carry Trot and Cap’n Bill swiftly across the ocean and bring them to the Giant’s Cave. They enjoy Trot’s visit and leave after helping her and Cap’n Bill return to their usual forms.

l: Pacific Ocean, The Sea Fairies, [Illustration: _Chap. 22._
s: The ocean carries the mermaids, Trot, and Cap’n Bill as they swim in a straight line through the middle water. They pass schools of fish and travel to the area where the Giant’s Cave entrance is near the sea bottom.

l: Giant's Cave, The Sea Fairies, [Illustration: _Chap. 22._
s: The Giant’s Cave is reached through a rocky entrance near the bottom of the sea, and its inner water is azure-blue. Trot and Cap’n Bill return to their boat inside the cave and leave through its mouth into the sunlight.

l: boat (Trot and Cap'n Bill's boat), The Sea Fairies, [Illustration: _Chap. 22._
s: Trot and Cap’n Bill find their little boat floating near the place where they left it in the Giant’s Cave. Cap’n Bill climbs aboard, brings Trot into it, and rows the boat toward and out of the cave.

l: return to their regular shapes, The Sea Fairies, [Illustration: _Chap. 22._
s: Princess Clia restores Trot and Cap’n Bill to their regular shapes at the surface of the cave’s water. Trot is again dressed normally with shoes and stockings, and Cap’n Bill has his flesh-and-hickory legs instead of a scaled tail.

l: Trot and Cap'n Bill's visit to the ocean palaces, The Sea Fairies, [Illustration: _Chap. 22._
s: Trot and Cap’n Bill’s visit ends safely after the mermaids transport them to the Giant’s Cave and restore their regular shapes. They thank and say goodbye to the mermaids, and Trot concludes that mortals know less than they think and are learning every day.

l: The Road to Oz
s: This document recounts Dorothy’s accidental journey toward Oz and Princess Ozma’s birthday celebration. Dorothy, Toto, and the Shaggy Man become lost after strange multiplying crossroads; the Shaggy Man carries a stolen Love Magnet that makes living things love him. On the road they acquire Button-Bright, a boy who answers nearly every question with “Don’t know,” and pass through Foxville, where King Dox gives Button-Bright a fox head and asks Dorothy for an invitation to Ozma’s party. In Dunkiton, King Kik-a-bray changes the Shaggy Man’s head into a donkey’s head, while Dorothy similarly promises him an invitation. The travelers are joined by Polychrome, the Rainbow’s Daughter, who has fallen from her father’s rainbow. They avoid the incessantly musical Allegro da Capo, then face capture by the Scoodlers, who intend to turn them into soup. Polychrome distracts a guard, enabling the Shaggy Man to defeat the Scoodlers by throwing their detachable heads into a black gulf. At the Deadly Desert, Johnny Dooit, summoned through the Love Magnet, builds a sand-boat that carries them into Oz. At the Truth Pond, Button-Bright and the Shaggy Man regain their proper human heads. In the Winkie country, Tik-Tok and Billina greet them on Ozma’s behalf. They visit Nick Chopper’s tin castle and Jack Pumpkinhead, then reach the Emerald City with the Cowardly Lion and Hungry Tiger. Ozma reveals that she arranged the roads that brought Dorothy to Oz and watched the journey through the Magic Picture. She forgives the Shaggy Man’s theft of the Love Magnet and places it above the Emerald City gates. The remainder centers on Ozma’s birthday. Dorothy welcomes arriving friends and foreign guests, including King Renard, Santa Claus, Queen Zixi, King Bud, and others. A grand banquet features food, magic, music, poetry, dance, and animal performances. The next day’s celebration includes a procession and many acts by the Wizard, Scarecrow, Tin Woodman, Glinda, Johnny Dooit, and Para Bruin. Giant soap bubbles send Button-Bright and Santa Claus home, Polychrome returns by rainbow, and Dorothy, Toto, and the Shaggy Man remain in Oz temporarily before Dorothy and Toto are later sent to Kansas by the Magic Belt.

l: Dorothy, The Road to Oz
s: Dorothy is a little Kansas girl and country girl who lives at Uncle Henry's farm-house and has Toto as her dog. She is also a traveler, a friend of Princess Ozma and many people in Oz, and is called a Princess of Oz and of the Emerald City. She has crossed the desert more than once: a cyclone first carried her across, the Silver Shoes returned her, and she later returns to Kansas by the Magic Belt. Her earlier Oz experiences include defeating a wicked witch with water, taking the Magic Belt from the Nome King, saving Tik-Tok and Billina, and becoming so well loved that Nick Chopper's tin castle holds life-size tin figures of her and Toto. Her journey begins when, while trying to direct the Shaggy Man toward Butterfield, changed crossroads leave her and Toto lost. She follows him down a strange road, meets the lost Button-Bright, and takes responsibility for him despite his inability to say where he belongs. With Toto, the Shaggy Man, Button-Bright, and later Polychrome, she travels through Foxville, Dunkiton, and dangerous country toward Oz and the Emerald City. She repeatedly trusts Ozma to help: to restore Button-Bright after he receives a fox's head, to send Polychrome home, and to help Dorothy return to Kansas. Captured by the Scoodlers, she escapes with the party, crosses the deadly desert in a sand-boat, and recognizes the Truth Pond, which restores her companions. In Oz, Dorothy reunites with Tik-Tok, Billina, Nick Chopper, the Cowardly Lion, and the Hungry Tiger. She is received with honor as Ozma's friend, stays at the Royal Palace, and dresses in a grey gown embroidered with silver. Ozma reveals that she guided Dorothy's route and watched the journey. Dorothy then receives guests for Ozma's birthday celebration, welcomes many visitors, and joins the procession with the Scarecrow. At the end, saddened by Button-Bright and Polychrome's departures, she chooses the Magic Belt over a bubble journey and is set to return to Kansas with Toto.

l: Shaggy Man, The Road to Oz
s: The Shaggy Man is a shaggy-clothed man, traveler, and Dorothy’s friend who calls himself good, despises money because it makes people proud and haughty, and wants love from everyone he meets. He carries the Love Magnet, which causes living things such as the foxes of Foxville to love him, though it does not protect him from the Scoodlers, who love him “in soup.” He begins as a stranger asking Dorothy about Butterfield while avoiding a man who owes him fifteen cents. He helps Dorothy when she is lost, proposes caring for the poor, lost Button-Bright, and joins Dorothy, Toto, Button-Bright, and later Polychrome on an uncertain journey, believing every road leads somewhere. He remains cheerful and practical, eating and sharing apples, refusing finer clothes because they would make him no longer the Shaggy Man, and protecting or aiding his companions. He is transformed by King Kik-a-bray into a man with a donkey head, dislikes it, and seeks the Truth Pond. Against the Scoodlers he leads the group, fights their guards, catches their thrown heads, and escapes with the others. When the party cannot cross the desert, he uses the Love Magnet to call Johnny Dooit and pilots the sand-boat across it. At the Truth Pond, his donkey head is removed and his proper shaggy human head restored. In the Land of Oz, he is impressed that money is not used and wishes to live there always. He is told he may stay if he proves himself honest, true, and worthy of friendship. At Ozma’s palace, unexpected welcome, fine shaggy clothes, jewels, and apartments astonish a man who has more often slept in hay-lofts and stables. Because bathing in the Truth Pond compels truth, he admits that he stole the Love Magnet from a girl in Butterfield after no one loved or cared for him. He agrees that it should hang over the Emerald City gates. After joining the reception and birthday procession, he remains in Oz while trying to prove himself honest and true.

l: Toto, The Road to Oz
s: Toto is Dorothy’s little black dog and companion: curious, lively, loyal, and often guided or restrained by her. He belongs to and is fond of Dorothy, communicates by wagging his tail, and travels with her, later returning with her to Kansas by the Magic Belt. He chases butterflies, birds, bees, and chickens, for which Uncle Henry disciplines him; he has more sense than Button-Bright, is known by Button-Bright as a former friend, and is friendly with the Cowardly Lion and Hungry Tiger. At the animals’ table he wears a bib and eats from a silver platter. Toto’s journey begins with the Shaggy Man putting him in a pocket after Toto attacks him. Released, Toto tries unsuccessfully to lead Dorothy home, then follows her and the Shaggy Man. He digs in Button-Bright’s hole, barks and tries to bite a fox-captain, befriends Polychrome, and growls at Allegro da Capo. Invisible among rocks, he barks at the Scoodlers but becomes frightened and crouches between Dorothy’s feet. He crosses the Deadly Desert in Dorothy’s arms, bites a donkey ear after a crash, and finally stays with Dorothy, barking at departing bubbles before returning to Kansas.

l: Butterfield, The Road to Oz
s: has road to Butterfield [the destination of the road] Butterfield is the place whose road Dorothy attempts to show the Shaggy Man. The Shaggy Man does not want to go there because a man who lives there owes him fifteen cents.

l: road to Butterfield, The Road to Oz
s: leads_to Butterfield Dorothy initially gives the Shaggy Man directions to the road to Butterfield and then leads him toward the branching roads. When they reach the crossroads, she points out the correct road, but the Shaggy Man deliberately starts along another one because he does not want to go to Butterfield.

l: the other roads, The Road to Oz
s: Stationary roads lead somewhere and meet at the farm-house; at Butterfield, five crossroads become many landmarkless roads, leaving Dorothy and Toto unable to find home until the Shaggy Man proposes the seventh.

l: getting lost, The Road to Oz
s: is_a state of disorientation [near Dorothy's home] Dorothy becomes lost after the roads and surrounding landmarks change while she is showing the Shaggy Man the way to Butterfield. She cannot identify the direction of the farm-house, and Toto is unable to lead her home.

l: the Love Magnet, The Road to Oz
s: The Love Magnet is a small, dull brown horseshoe-shaped piece of metal, kept wrapped in paper and tied with cotton string. It is a charm that makes every living thing its bearer meets love the bearer, especially causing those near or encountering the Shaggy Man to love him. It makes Button-Bright, King Dox, the foxes, the Scoodlers, and the travelers love the Shaggy Man, and may help him gain King Kik-a-bray's affection after his transformation. The Shaggy Man uses it to summon Johnny Dooit, a powerful friend who loves him because he owns it. He later admits stealing it from a girl in Butterfield because he wanted love. Rather than give it to Dorothy, Button-Bright, or the Wizard, he agrees it should hang above the Emerald City gates, causing love for whoever enters or leaves.

l: Kansas, The Road to Oz
s: Kansas is an unromantic state containing a farm-house and Uncle Henry's farm; Dorothy believes she is there after leaving the farm, but King Dox corrects her.

l: Hungry Tiger, The Road to Oz
s: Hungry Tiger is a large, striped tiger with a conscience that rules him like a tyrant. Sent by Ozma and harnessed with the Cowardly Lion to her royal chariot, he meets Dorothy near the Emerald City, jokes about eating fat babies and Polychrome, but cannot act on such desires. He then greets Dorothy's companions and draws the chariot to the Royal Palace.

l: money, The Road to Oz
s: makes people [proud and haughty] Money is not used or known in the Land of Oz. Nick Chopper says that relying on money instead of love, kindness, and the desire to please one another would make Oz no better than the rest of the world.

l: Button-Bright, The Road to Oz
s: Button-Bright is a little boy, prettily dressed in sailor clothes, with curls, short legs, and a sailor hat. Though his mother calls him Button-Bright because his father said he was bright as a button, he does not know his real name, home, origin, or how he came to be lost on the seventh road. His people love him and take pains with his appearance, but worry because he is lost. He is younger than Dorothy and becomes her travelling companion and friend, joining Dorothy, the Shaggy Man, and Toto after Dorothy finds him digging a large hole beneath a chestnut tree. He is curious, clever, and repeatedly answers difficult questions with uncertainty, often saying that he does not know. He asks many questions, enjoys Foxville and its royal drum, likes Allegro da Capo and his music, and is interested in strange sights and events. He eats readily, especially pie, but fears being made into soup when the Scoodlers capture the travelers. During their escape and further journey, he is sometimes frightened, hungry, weary, tearful, or hurt, but continues with the group. In Foxville, King Dox changes his head into a little fox head. Button-Bright cries at first, though praise from the fox-princesses partly comforts him. He remains a boy, not a fox, and travels in his sailor suit with the fox head hidden or covered by his sailor hat. In Dunkiton, others mistake him for a fox. His fox head is later stuck in a gopher hole after the sand-boat crashes, but he is pulled free. At the Truth Pond, he is frightened by his reflection, falls into the water, and regains his proper chubby face, blue eyes, and curls. He reaches the Emerald City, grows less afraid of the Cowardly Lion and Hungry Tiger, meets Ozma and other guests, and is recognized by Santa Claus as a boy whose home he has visited. After the birthday celebration, Button-Bright asks to go home. The Wizard sends him westward in a giant soap bubble, where he sits cross-legged and waves his sailor hat as he returns to Kansas.

l: the seventh road, The Road to Oz
s: A pleasant road curves through green meadows, daisy and buttercup fields, and shady trees, with no houses or visible creatures for some distance, leading Dorothy, the Shaggy Man, and Toto to Button-Bright.

l: journey to the Emerald City, The Road to Oz
s: This is a journey toward the Emerald City and the Land of Oz, undertaken by Dorothy and companions while Dorothy intends to find Princess Ozma. After spending a night in Foxville, Dorothy, Button-Bright, and the Shaggy Man resume travel, promise to seek Princess Ozma, and are escorted toward an unknown village. Toto and Polychrome travel with Dorothy, Shaggy Man, and Button-Bright; Polychrome joins to keep warm and seek a way home. The road takes them through Dunkiton, where they stay overnight, then through green fields, groves, and unknown country. They encounter Allegro da Capo, leave the Truth Pond after Button-Bright and the Shaggy Man are restored, and seek directions. After meeting Tik-Tok and Billina, they continue toward the Emerald City, planning to stop at Nick Chopper's new castle before arriving the following day.

l: King Dox, The Road to Oz
s: King Dox, whose private name is Dox and who is also called King Dox, is a wise fox and king of Foxville. He rules as Foxville’s sovereign and, with his wife, receives Dorothy, Button-Bright, and the shaggy man in his royal palace. He welcomes them, explains Foxville’s location in relation to Oz and Kansas, recognizes Dorothy’s importance, changes Button-Bright’s head into a fox’s head, and entertains the travelers with dinner and a theater performance. He asks Dorothy for an invitation to Princess Ozma’s birthday celebration and hopes to cross the Dreadful Desert to the Emerald City if invited.

l: fox-captain, The Road to Oz
s: Captain of the fox-soldiers, he first surrounds Dorothy's party as prisoners, then the Love Magnet makes him friendly; he escorts them to King Dox and advises them.

l: the fox soldiers, The Road to Oz
s: Fox soldiers are uniformed foxes who guard the road from Foxville to a neighboring beast village. Wearing colorful clothing and carrying toothed wooden swords, they surround Dorothy's party and escort it through Foxville to the royal palace.

l: the foxes of Foxville, The Road to Oz
s: The foxes of Foxville are civilized foxes living in a richly decorated city, wearing elaborate feather clothing and eating fowl. They come out to observe strangers, serve in the royal palace, and love the Shaggy Man because of the Love Magnet. They honor Button-Bright, host the travelers with a meal, play, rooms, and breakfast, then escort them out while remaining watchful of a neighboring village.

l: Foxville, The Road to Oz
s: Foxville is a fine, big, beautiful city in Fairyland, nearer to Oz than Kansas. It has marble houses decorated with birds and fox heads, a royal palace, and a fox theater. Ruled by King Dox and King Renard the Fourth, its civilized fox inhabitants welcome travelers, who stay overnight and leave through an arch.

l: Royal Palace, The Road to Oz
s: Royal Palace is a magnificent royal palace, described as standing in central Foxville and as a royal residence in the Emerald City. Marked by a crowned fox’s head, it has richly decorated rooms, fox servants, and a golden throne room where King Dox receives travelers. It is vast and elegant, surrounded by gardens and ample grounds behind a green-marble wall. Dorothy and companions arrive in Ozma’s chariot, are welcomed by servants, and receive prepared rooms; its interiors include halls, drawing-rooms, guest apartments, and the shaggy man’s lavish quarters.

l: Princess Ozma, The Road to Oz
s: Princess Ozma is the princess and girl Ruler of Oz, ruling the Land of Oz, including the Emerald City and all four countries. She is Dorothy's friend, a gracious and beautiful ruler who inspires love rather than fear or ordinary admiration; at her banquet she is admired as dignified and bewitching. She possesses the Magic Picture, through which she watches travelers, and the Magic Belt, used for rescue and transport. She also owns the royal chariot, though she chooses not to ride it during her public birthday procession. Her past includes living with Mombi in the shape of a boy, fleeing with a pepper-box containing the Powder of Life, and witnessing that Powder bring Jack Pumpkinhead to life. Ozma built Jack's body, carved his pumpkin head, and brought him to life with Magic Powder, so Jack considers her his parent. She later used the remaining Powder of Life to bring the Flying Gump to life. The records chiefly follow preparations for Ozma's birthday. While busy organizing the celebration, she watches Dorothy and her companions, sends Tik-Tok and Billina to welcome them, and sends the Cowardly Lion and Hungry Tiger to meet Dorothy because she may be weary. She has arranged roads to guide Dorothy toward Oz, invites Dorothy to the Emerald City, and prepares a welcome for her friends and guests. She orders luxurious apartments, clothing, ornaments, and comforts for the shaggy man, eagerly welcomes Dorothy, and expects her friends for dinner after rest. Ozma invites rulers and guests to a grand party and banquet, asks Dorothy to receive arrivals while she oversees preparations, and receives many birthday presents. As honored hostess, she greets the guests at the royal banquet, where they drink to her health and happiness. On the anniversary of her birth, she leads a public procession and entertainment outside the Emerald City, walking with subjects and guests and receiving their good wishes. At the end, she agrees that Dorothy and Toto will be transported to Kansas while Dorothy sleeps.

l: the Land of Oz, The Road to Oz
s: The Land of Oz is a beautiful fairy land beyond the Deadly Sands, containing the Emerald City, which lies somewhere in its middle and is its only town or village. It is divided into four parts: the purple Country of the Gillikins in the north, the blue Country of the Munchkins in the east, the red Country of the Quadlings in the south, and the yellow Country of the Winkies in the west. Ozma rules the whole land, while each country has a smaller ruler. What most distinguishes Oz is its happiness and social values. Money is unknown, so there are neither rich nor poor; inhabitants try to give one another what they want, and people are valued for themselves, kindness, and good deeds. Animals receive as much consideration as people when they behave themselves. Nobody ordinarily dies, though bad people may be condemned and killed by good citizens. The Truth Pond is somewhere in Oz, though its exact location is unknown. The account first presents Oz as the destination sought by travelers, nearer than Kansas but blocked by the Deadly Sands. After they cross the desert, they recognize the grassy, tree-covered tableland as part of Oz and set out for the Emerald City. Oz then becomes the setting for Ozma's birthday: guests gather at her palace, Santa Claus visits the Emerald City, and a royal banquet brings together people and creatures from many places. The account ends with people from all four parts of Oz arriving in the Emerald City, represented by their rulers, to cheer a procession and watch the birthday entertainments.

l: Emerald City, The Road to Oz
s: Emerald City is the magnificent, stately central city of the Land of Oz, located where the four countries meet and ruled by Princess Ozma. It is the only city or village in the Land of Oz and contains the royal palace and the Royal College, headed by Mr. H. M. Woggle-Bug, T.E. High emerald walls, spires, domes, jewel-studded gates, gold-covered and emerald-set buildings, polished marble sidewalks, and a surrounding green meadow define it. Its people are richly dressed, happy, and contented. It is repeatedly the travelers' destination: Dorothy expects Ozma and her friends there to help Polychrome and others, while the group journeys there for Ozma's birthday. They are invited onward, expect to arrive after a night at Nick Chopper's castle, and Jack Pumpkinhead plans to join them there. The city welcomes the Scarecrow with crowds, trumpets, and a brass band. For Ozma's birthday, crowds fill its streets; a procession travels from the royal palace through the gates to a pavilion in the green fields and returns. Ozma orders the Love Magnet hung above the gates so all who enter or leave may be loved and loving.

l: Princess Ozma's birthday celebration, The Road to Oz
s: Princess Ozma's birthday celebration is a planned royal function, scheduled for the twenty-first and intended as the grandest and most brilliant ceremony in Fairyland. It honors Ozma and is arranged on the broad green outside the Emerald City gates so all her people can attend without crowding. As preparations proceed, Dorothy and her companions travel to reach the party, while Nick Chopper is polished; King Dox and King Kik-a-bray seek invitations. Invited guests arrive the day before, including Santa Claus, Queen Zixi of Ix, the royal family of Ev, other rulers, and unusual visitors, bringing many presents. A grand evening banquet gathers the visitors, with the Wizard's magic exhibition planned afterward. The banquet is presented as only the introduction to the birthday celebration, which is scheduled for the following morning.

l: Dorothy's fairy adventure, The Road to Oz
s: Dorothy's fairy adventure brings her and the Shaggy Man unexpectedly to Foxville, where she suspects magical help but he denies causing it.

l: the Magic Belt, The Road to Oz
s: The Magic Belt is a magical object left with Ozma that works in fairy countries, transports foreign visitors to the Emerald City, and is planned to return Dorothy and Toto to Kansas.

l: the Deadly Desert, The Road to Oz
s: The Deadly Desert is a vast, gray, dismal, barren waste that separates and lies before the Land of Oz. Its uneven, billowing sand turns living flesh to dust, blocking travelers who touch it. The travelers find it in their path, then Johnny Dooit provides a sand-boat whose runners and sail prevent contact, allowing them to cross its dangerous, rocking surface at great speed.

l: Button-Bright's fox head, The Road to Oz
s: Button-Bright's fox head, with sharp nose, pointed ears, and keen little eyes, replaces his curls, round face, and blue eyes; he cries and dislikes it, foxes praise it, and Dorothy believes Princess Ozma can restore it.

l: Button-Bright's transformation, The Road to Oz
s: Button-Bright's transformation begins when King Dox, King Renard the Fourth, waves his paw and replaces the boy's human head with a fox head. The King cannot undo it, worrying Dorothy and the shaggy man, though foxes consider it an honor. Later, Button-Bright falls into the Truth Pond, which reverses the change and restores his original appearance.

l: Polychrome, The Road to Oz
s: Polychrome, also called Polly, is the beautiful Daughter of the Rainbow: radiant and fairy-shapely, with flowing spun-gold hair and gauzy, fleecy, rainbow-hued robes striped in violet, rose, topaz, olive, azure, and white. She is the daughter of Polychrome's father and fell or slid from her father's rainbow, becoming lost, afraid, worried, and lonely on the road. She joins Dorothy's group to seek help and regains a cheerful mood as they travel. What matters most to her is her distinctive rainbow nature: she dances often, sometimes to keep warm, enjoys beautiful colors, and prefers freshly gathered dewdrops and mist-cakes to ordinary food. At luncheon and later dinners she eats little, misses mist-cakes, and asks for dewdrops, mist-cakes, or cloudbuns. She dances along the road, to music, and for banquet guests; she also warns the group about a nearby city and asks whether the road leads to the Emerald City. She stays close to Dorothy when frightened by the Scoodlers, is captured with the others, and helps create an escape opportunity by slapping a guard and moving away quickly. Crossing the desert, she clings to the bow, sees the green tableland ahead, and warns the shaggy man to slow down; her gown tears in the crash, but she is unhurt. Near the Emerald City she admires rainbow-colored leaves, is frightened by the Lion and Tiger until Dorothy introduces them, then delights in the city's beauty and rides in Ozma's royal chariot.

l: the Rainbow, The Road to Oz
s: The Rainbow is Polychrome’s home and father, stretched across the country with one end on a lonely road. Polychrome slides down from it; it melts when she grasps it. Later it descends at a celebration, lifts her skyward, and fades after she merges with its colors.

l: lonely road, The Road to Oz
s: The lonely road is the only road in its part of the country, running through empty fields and groves. It begins as a place where Polychrome is found dancing and weeping, then becomes rough and uneven across a rocky plain toward low mountains, seeming to end at rocks where Scoodlers block it.

l: Polychrome's dance, The Road to Oz
s: is_a dance [performed to keep warm] Polychrome's dance is graceful and whirling, and she says she began it to keep warm after becoming lost. Later, her dancing and laughter enliven the group's journey.

l: Scarecrow, The Road to Oz
s: Scarecrow is an alive man, made by a Munchkin farmer and stuffed with straw or oat-straw, with no appetite and unable to eat. Popular and beloved in the Land of Oz, he seeks fresh straw in Munchkin Country. He arrives on a decorated wooden Saw-Horse, helps Dorothy receive guests, joins her procession, performs sword-swallowing, and stays for dinner and evening.

l: Tin Woodman, The Road to Oz
s: Tin Woodman, also named Nick Chopper, is an alive metal person made entirely of tin and the Emperor and ruler of the Country of the Winkies. Once cut apart by his axe and rebuilt in tin, he received an excellent heart from the Wizard of Oz. That heart grows softer and kinder, matching his kindly, simple nature: he loves everyone, is loved by everyone, and is happy. He lives in a new tin castle, carries a tin-plated, diamond-set axe, and welcomes Dorothy and her companions there with a feast before traveling with them toward the Emerald City. Along the way he explains that Jack Pumpkinhead remains alive, discusses Jack's brighter new pumpkin head, and recounts the Powder of Life's history and uses, while approving that the powder is gone. In the Emerald City he greets the Cowardly Lion and Hungry Tiger, explains that Oz's people work only half their time, cleans dust from his shining body in his usual Royal Palace room, and stands at the right of the throne during a reception. He welcomes Tik-tok, is Tik-tok's friend, and joins a love song with everyone in the chorus.

l: the donkeys of Dunkiton, The Road to Oz
s: The donkeys of Dunkiton are a clever, adorned group with hoof-like limbs that use front legs as arms. Afraid of foxes, they make a racket by kicking suspended metal sheets. They mistake Button-Bright for a fox, but the shaggy man corrects them; they stop and agree to lead the travelers to King Kik-a-bray.

l: King Kik-a-bray, The Road to Oz
s: King Kik-a-bray is the exalted ruler of the donkeys in Dunkiton, wearing a golden crown and wielding a jeweled magic staff. He greets travelers according to their stations, uses the staff to give the shaggy man a donkey’s head, directs him to the Truth Pond for restoration, supplies food and lodging, and asks Dorothy for an invitation to Ozma’s birthday celebration.

l: Dunkiton, The Road to Oz
s: Dunkiton is a large walled town inhabited by donkeys, with whitewashed houses scattered irregularly and a road passing through an open gate. Its donkeys call it the center of the world's highest civilization, though Dorothy considers them stupid beasts. Ruled by King Kik-a-bray, it uses metal sheets and loud kicking to drive away foxes; travelers stay one night before continuing.

l: the grey donkey, The Road to Oz
s: guides the visitors [through Dunkiton] The grey donkey leads the travelers through Dunkiton and explains the city's customs, including hoof fortune-telling and the donkeys' lack of formal schools. He introduces the travelers to King Kik-a-bray.

l: donkeys, The Road to Oz
s: Dunkiton donkeys consider themselves civilized and wise, favor experience over formal schooling, live in scattered houses, paint with tails, eat bran, oats, hay, and grass, and reject streets, numbered houses, and schools.

l: Truth Pond, The Road to Oz
s: Truth Pond is a crystal, glass-still pond in a tree circle in the Country of the Winkies, somewhere in the Land of Oz. Its water restores altered appearances, giving Button-Bright his original face and the Shaggy Man his proper head after a donkey-head transformation. It also compels the Shaggy Man to tell the truth, leading him to admit he lied to Dorothy about the Love Magnet.

l: the shaggy man's donkey-head transformation, The Road to Oz
s: is_caused_by the donkey king's magic [performed by waving the jeweled staff] King Kik-a-bray changes the shaggy man's human head into a brown, shaggy donkey head with long ears. The transformation cannot be undone by the King's magic, and the shaggy man must bathe in the Truth Pond to reverse it.

l: the travelers, The Road to Oz
s: The travelers cross the Deadly Desert by sand-boat seeking the Emerald City, survive a crash onto a grassy tableland, and search for people to guide them.

l: Allegro da Capo, The Road to Oz
s: Allegro da Capo is a little fat man and self-described famous musicker who lives alone beside the road. Bald, blue-eyed, and elaborately dressed, he carries a stout gold-headed cane. Reeds in his lungs make involuntary, error-free music whenever he breathes, so he calls himself a band. Musical since life began, he wants to accompany the travelers to Princess Ozma's birthday performance, but they leave him behind because his constant music troubles them.

l: music, The Road to Oz
s: has_charms soothing savage [according to Allegro da Capo] Music comes from Allegro da Capo as queer, organ-like sounds and later accompanies his sung replies. The travelers hear it until they pass over a hill, after which the sound gradually dies away.

l: the musicker's involuntary music, The Road to Oz
s: is_caused_by Allegro da Capo [his breathing] The musicker's involuntary music is produced whenever Allegro da Capo breathes because he says his lungs are full of reeds. He cannot stop it, and the travelers find its continual piping difficult to endure.

l: Ozma's birthday, The Road to Oz
s: Ozma's birthday celebration in the Emerald City, with ceremonies in the green fields, is prepared through arriving guests and their presents. It culminates in a large public procession and varied entertainment, music, magic, juggling, dancing, flying, and giant soap bubbles, attended by foreign guests and Oz citizens before the guests depart home.

l: Scoodlers, The Road to Oz
s: Scoodlers are slender, hostile creatures living on rocks around a hollow in the hills and in the Scoodlers' cave, ruled by the Queen of the Scoodlers. Each has two fronts and no back, alternating black and white sides with different faces and yellow or purple hair, small sparkling eyes, T-shaped feet, and a removable head. They surround Dorothy and the travelers, demand them for soup, and attack by throwing their heads. After capturing the travelers and taking them to the Soup Kettle to chop them and make soup, they lose their heads to the Shaggy Man and become helpless.

l: the soup, The Road to Oz
s: is_made_from prisoners [as intended by the Scoodlers] The Scoodlers intend to make soup from the captured travelers. They plan to flavor it with potatoes, carrots, onions, turnips, garlic, salt, and red pepper, but the soup is never made.

l: the Queen of the Scoodlers, The Road to Oz
s: The Queen of the Scoodlers rules the Scoodlers. Lean and bony, with fiery red and bright yellow sides, two faces, and a dented, twisted silver crown, she orders captives through a meat chopper and seasons soup before the shaggy man throws her head into the black gulf.

l: the prisoners, The Road to Oz
s: are_captives_of the Scoodlers The prisoners are led into the Scoodlers' cave and confined in a storehouse containing vegetables for soup. They escape when Polychrome distracts the guard, then cross the narrow bridge while the shaggy man holds off the Scoodlers.

l: the Scoodlers' cave, The Road to Oz
s: The Scoodlers' cave is an immense hollow dome inside a mountain, with roof holes, rock houses around a circular space, and the central Soup Kettle; beyond its narrow bridge lies a deep gulf.

l: the narrow bridge, The Road to Oz
s: A rock bridge across a deep gulf connects the Scoodlers' cave to an outside path, enabling Dorothy and companions to escape.

l: the black gulf, The Road to Oz
s: is_a deep gulf [beneath the bridge] The black gulf is a deep chasm below the narrow bridge. The shaggy man throws the Scoodlers' heads into it, including the Queen's head.

l: the Soup Kettle, The Road to Oz
s: A huge iron kettle hangs by a stout chain in the Scoodlers' cave, with kindling and shavings beneath it ready to cook prisoners into soup.

l: Scoodler heads, The Road to Oz
s: Scoodler heads, each with two pairs of eyes, are removable weapons; thrown at the shaggy man, he catches and sends them into the black gulf.

l: the Scoodlers' capture of the travelers, The Road to Oz
s: The Scoodlers surround the travelers after knocking them down with thrown heads and lead them across the narrow bridge into the cave. They bring the captives before the Queen and confine them in a storehouse while preparing to make soup.

l: the escape from the Scoodlers, The Road to Oz
s: is_completed successfully [the travelers reach the road] The escape begins when Polychrome distracts the guard and the shaggy man traps the guard's head in a sack. The group runs from the cave and crosses the narrow bridge while the shaggy man stops the pursuing Scoodlers.

l: the Scoodlers' defeat, The Road to Oz
s: is_caused_by the shaggy man [by removing their heads] The Scoodlers are defeated when the shaggy man catches every head they throw and casts the heads into the black gulf. Their headless bodies are left wriggling helplessly in the cave, unable to bother the travelers or anyone else.

l: Polychrome, The Road to Oz
s: Polychrome is the Rainbow's Daughter, a cloud fairy and traveler who lives on the rainbow among fleecy clouds, where magic has no use. She wishes for her father to find her and offers rainbow life to travelers, while watching Johnny Dooit build a sand-boat. Nick Chopper calls her the loveliest vision his tin eyes have seen; she eats dewdrops and dances gracefully. She greets Ozma without jealousy, delights in the Wizard's piglets, joins Oz's birthday procession, and finally dances up a settling rainbow to return to her father, melting into its colors.

l: Johnny Dooit, The Road to Oz
s: Johnny Dooit is a hard-working workman with grey hair and long grey whiskers, carrying tools in a copper chest. Called by the Shaggy Man using the Love Magnet, he appears, is said to be able to do anything, and quickly builds a twelve-foot sand-boat. After teaching the Shaggy Man to sail it, he disappears with his tools.

l: the Deadly Sands, The Road to Oz
s: turn living flesh to dust [in an instant] The Deadly Sands are said to turn any living flesh that touches them into dust instantly. They prevent anyone from reaching the Land of Oz by walking across the desert.

l: the sand-boat, The Road to Oz
s: The sand-boat is a twelve-foot-long, four-foot-wide boat designed to travel over sand. Built at the edge of the Deadly Desert by Johnny Dooit from boards, a pole, rope, and canvas, it has two sharp runners, a pointed front, a mast and sail, and a stern rudder. Its runners and sails let wind carry travelers over the Deadly Sands without contact with them, provided it does not tip. It glides rapidly across the desert, then strikes rocks at the far edge, is crushed into splinters, and loses its sail to a tall tree.

l: the journey across the desert, The Road to Oz
s: The journey across the desert is a crossing that cannot be made on foot because the sands destroy living flesh. Johnny Dooit builds a sand-boat; wind drives it rapidly over the sand until it crashes at the rocks and ends on the grassy tableland.

l: the sand-boat's crash, The Road to Oz
s: The sand-boat's crash occurs at rocks on the desert's edge when the shaggy man cannot lower the sail, throwing Dorothy, Button-Bright, Toto, Polychrome, and the shaggy man onto grass unharmed except for minor mishaps.

l: Cowardly Lion, The Road to Oz
s: The Cowardly Lion is a large, tawny animal who is not actually cowardly and has received courage from the Wizard. With the Hungry Tiger, he guards Princess Ozma and draws her royal chariot. Sent by Ozma, he meets Dorothy near the Emerald City, reports that they are well and happy, welcomes her companions and Polychrome, gently pats Toto, and brings Dorothy into the City for Ozma's grand party.

l: Wizard of Oz, The Road to Oz
s: Wizard of Oz, a magician famous as a humbug magician, lives in Emerald City and is loved by all the people of Oz. He once gave courage to Cowardly Lion and owns eight trained piglets. At Ozma’s palace he affectionately greets Dorothy and entertains with the piglets; later, as Princess Ozma’s Master of Ceremonies, he juggles, introduces acts, operates bubbles, and sends guests home.

l: Winkies, The Road to Oz
s: The Winkies inhabit the Country of the Winkies, living among neat yellow houses and scattered farmhouses. Freed by Dorothy after the wicked witch’s defeat, they become skilled tinsmiths, build Nick Chopper’s castle, love him as Emperor, and cheer him with a tin-instrument orchestra.

l: Country of the Winkies, The Road to Oz
s: Yellow place ruled by Tin Woodman, with river boundary at Emerald City; Dorothy and companions meet Tik-Tok and Billina en route there.

l: Shaggy Man's restoration, The Road to Oz
s: restored Shaggy Man's proper head [through immersion in the Truth Pond] The Shaggy Man's donkey head is removed when he dives into the Truth Pond. His own shaggy head and whiskers return, and he is pleased to look like himself again.

l: the Truth Pond's power to restore appearances, The Road to Oz
s: The Truth Pond restores people’s proper appearances when they enter its water, changing Button-Bright’s fox head back to his original face and the Shaggy Man’s donkey head back to his own head.

l: Tik-tok, The Road to Oz
s: Tik-Tok is a burnished copper, clock-work man and machine powered by machinery, with a winding key on his back. Though not alive, his machinery lets him function like a living being. A trustworthy, reliable friend of Dorothy and the Tin Woodman, he lives in the Royal Palace. Princess Ozma sends him to welcome Dorothy and the travelers; when his thought and speech run down, Dorothy winds him, and he guides them toward the Emerald City.

l: Billina, The Road to Oz
s: Billina is a yellow hen with fluffy feathers and a pearl necklace, head and parent of ten chicks all named Dorothy. Dorothy is her dearest friend; Billina knows Cowardly Lion and Hungry Tiger and is sent by Princess Ozma to welcome Dorothy. She reunites with Dorothy, describes her chicks and Tik-Tok, then enters the Throne-Room with the chicks and gathers them.

l: tin castle (Nick Chopper's castle), The Road to Oz
s: Nick Chopper's new tin castle was built because the old castle was damp and might rust his tin body. Shining from a hilltop, it has towers, steeples, domes, gables, flower-beds, fountains, and rooms whose furniture, floors, and walls are brightly polished tin. Its grounds display life-size tin statues of his friends, including Dorothy with Toto at her feet, and it contains a grand tin dining-hall for entertaining guests.

l: Miss Polly, The Road to Oz
s: travels_with Dorothy [to Oz] Polly joins Dorothy, the shaggy man, Button-Bright, and Toto for breakfast. She sits beside Dorothy during the reception of the invited guests and is kissed by Glinda the Good.

l: love and kindness, The Road to Oz
s: Love and kindness, together with the desire to please one another, replace money in the Land of Oz. Nick Chopper presents these qualities as the reason there are no rich or poor people and as the basis of their happiness. The shaggy man steals the Love Magnet because he wants to be loved, while the girl in Butterfield is unhappy because too many young men love her. Ozma teaches that in Oz people are loved for themselves, their kindness to one another, and their good deeds, and she plans to spread love through the Love Magnet at the Emerald City's gates.

l: tin dinner, The Road to Oz
s: A plentiful dinner is served in the grand tin dining-hall at tin castle on polished tin dishes, accompanied by a Winkie orchestra. Toto eats beside Dorothy; Nick Chopper eats nothing; Polychrome tastes dewdrops, eats little, and dances afterward.

l: Emperor's departure for the Emerald City, The Road to Oz
s: includes Nick Chopper [he traveled with Dorothy and her companions] The morning after the feast, Nick Chopper leaves his tin castle with Dorothy and the others and travels toward the Emerald City. He has been brightly polished and carries his tin-plated, diamond-set axe, while the Winkies assemble at the gates and cheer him as he departs.

l: the pumpkin-field, The Road to Oz
s: A large field in the yellow country of the Winkies, where Jack Pumpkinhead lives and raises remarkably large pumpkins.

l: pumpkins, The Road to Oz
s: Some pumpkins in the field are remarkably large. Jack uses pumpkins for his heads, and pumpkins that are too large for heads can be hollowed out for other purposes.

l: Jack Pumpkinhead, The Road to Oz
s: Jack Pumpkinhead is an alive pumpkin-headed man created by Ozma and brought to life by the Magic Powder. With a clumsily jointed wooden body and a carved yellow pumpkin head, he lives in the pumpkin-field, farms pumpkins, owns a pumpkin house and private graveyard, buries spoiled heads, and plans to follow travelers to the Emerald City for Ozma's party.

l: Jack Pumpkinhead's pumpkin house, The Road to Oz
s: Jack Pumpkinhead's house is a monstrous hollow pumpkin shell, cut with a door and windows, fitted with stovepipe and six steps, and expected to last long.

l: the Magic Powder, The Road to Oz
s: The Powder of Life, invented by a crooked Sorcerer, brings things to life. It animated Jack Pumpkinhead, the Saw-Horse, Flying Gump, and, when Dyna unknowingly sprinkled it on a blue bear rug, the rug; it is then completely used up.

l: Jack Pumpkinhead's farming, The Road to Oz
s: includes_growing pumpkins [to maintain a supply of heads] Jack began raising pumpkins after once having to wear an old head longer than was healthy because pumpkins were out of season. He now plants pumpkin seeds and waters young vines so that he will always have a replacement head.

l: Ozma's royal chariot, The Road to Oz
s: is_a golden chariot [decorated with emeralds and lined with green and gold satin] Ozma's royal chariot is a splendid golden vehicle decorated with clusters of sparkling emeralds, lined with green and gold satin, and furnished with green plush cushions embroidered with a crown and monogram. The Cowardly Lion and Hungry Tiger draw it into the Emerald City, carrying Dorothy, Button-Bright, and Polychrome to the Royal Palace.

l: the shaggy man's welcome, The Road to Oz
s: is_a welcome [a royal welcome for a guest] The shaggy man's welcome is marked by respectful service and extraordinary comfort. A servant conducts him to his apartments, invites him to make himself at home, and promises to lead him to the drawing-room to meet Princess Ozma.

l: the royal palace, The Road to Oz
s: has the palace balcony [at its front] The royal palace hosts Dorothy's breakfast, the reception of the invited guests, and the presentation of Ozma's birthday presents. Its front balcony overlooks the City, and its rooms accommodate distinguished visitors such as Glinda the Good.

l: the Throne-Room, The Road to Oz
s: is_a room [of the royal palace] The Throne-Room is where Dorothy receives Ozma's invited guests. Dorothy sits in Ozma's seat there, with Polly and Button-Bright beside her and several familiar figures positioned around the throne.

l: Glinda the Sorceress, The Road to Oz
s: is_a Sorceress [powerful and kind] Glinda the Good arrives as an important sorceress and is described as both kind and powerful. She greets Dorothy lovingly, kisses Button-Bright and Polly, smiles upon the shaggy man, and is taken to a magnificent room with fifty servants assigned to wait upon her.

l: John Dough, The Road to Oz
s: King John Dough, an edible gingerbread ruler of Hiland and Loland, arrives at Ozma's royal banquet worried visitors may eat him. Assured of safety by the Scarecrow, he gives Ozma his pearl-decorated gingerbread crown, a birthday present.

l: Chick the Cherub, The Road to Oz
s: Chick the Cherub, an Incubator Baby without parents, arrives as King John Dough's Head Boolywag and Para Bruin's faithful friend, warmly greets the guests, presents the crown, and is escorted to rooms.

l: Para Bruin, The Road to Oz
s: Para Bruin is King John Dough's rubber bear and faithful friend, an animal who walks upright on hind feet, is bouncy, and has twinkling black eyes. He arrives from Hiland and Loland and remarks on the queer assembled company.

l: the invited guests, The Road to Oz
s: arrive_at the Throne-Room [for reception by Dorothy] The invited guests arrive at the royal palace for Ozma's birthday celebrations. Dorothy receives them in the Throne-Room, while the High Chamberlain announces their names and escorts them to their rooms.

l: the reception of the guests, The Road to Oz
s: occurs_in the Throne-Room [with Dorothy acting for Ozma] The reception of the guests takes place in the Throne-Room with Dorothy acting for Ozma. Familiar residents and foreign visitors are greeted, introduced, and made welcome before the High Chamberlain escorts them to their rooms.

l: Santa Claus, The Road to Oz
s: Santa Claus is an immortal saint, a mighty and loyal friend of children, with a round body and a red ermine-trimmed cloak. He keeps reindeer at home, owns and loves the Ryls and Knooks, and visits children on Christmas Eve. At Princess Ozma's birthday celebration, he arrives with the Ryls and Knooks, brings Ozma presents, recognizes Dorothy and Button-Bright, and promises to tell Polychrome's father where she is. Because the weather is too warm for his reindeer, he rides the Saw-Horse around the Emerald City. At Ozma's banquet he is the jolliest and most important guest, sits in the seat of honor, and offers a verse toast to Ozma. In the procession he tosses toys to children, directs guests' bubble journeys, and rides home with his companions in soap bubbles.

l: Queen Zixi of Ix, The Road to Oz
s: Queen Zixi, exquisite queen of Ix, rules from a golden throne and possesses perpetual youth despite having lived thousands of years. Appearing about sixteen, she arrives with King Bud of Noland and Princess Fluff at Princess Ozma's birthday celebration, where Dorothy admires her beauty.

l: royal banquet, The Road to Oz
s: The royal banquet, held for Ozma's birthday, opens the birthday celebration in the palace's great dining-hall. Guests feast at decorated tables while performances include an ode, magical pie, Rainbow Dance, songs, drills, dances, and bouncing; it continues until late evening before the next day's celebration.

l: the birthday procession, The Road to Oz
s: The birthday procession is a Birthday Celebration in Oz. Young girls carrying roses lead, followed by the four rulers, Emerald City Cornet Band, Royal Army, Princess Ozma, and notable companions including Santa Claus, Dorothy and the Scarecrow, Toto, and the Wizard. Foreign guests, familiar figures, servants, and Oz people join before it passes through the emerald gates.

l: the Wizard's soap-bubble machine, The Road to Oz
s: A machine hidden beneath a platform uses a soapsuds tank, glue, and air-pumps to blow huge, durable bubbles that float for hours without breaking.

l: the giant soap bubbles, The Road to Oz
s: Giant soap bubbles, tough from rapidly drying glue, float upward in sunshine with iridescent colors, carrying people or smaller bubbles safely through the sky for hours.

l: the bubble journeys, The Road to Oz
s: transport Button-Bright [westward toward his family] The bubble journeys begin when the Queen of Merryland travels away in a bubble, followed by Princess Fluff, King Bud, Queen Zixi, and other foreign guests. Button-Bright and Santa Claus also depart this way, with Santa Claus directing the travelers toward their homes.

l: the Rainbow's Daughter's return home, The Road to Oz
s: is_a return journey [along the Rainbow] The Rainbow's Daughter, Polychrome, returns home by dancing upward along the rainbow. Dorothy believes Polychrome is better off with her father because the Land of Oz cannot be like home to a cloud fairy.

l: The Emerald City of Oz
s: This document is an Oz fairy tale framed by L. Frank Baum’s note that children’s letters and ideas have helped shape the adventures of Dorothy, Aunt Em, Uncle Henry, and others. It begins with Roquat the Red, the Nome King, furious that Dorothy possesses his Magic Belt. Seeking revenge, he orders a secret tunnel dug beneath the Deadly Desert and sends General Guph to recruit the Whimsies, Growleywogs, and Phanfasms for an invasion of Oz. Meanwhile, Dorothy’s Kansas relatives face the loss of their farm. Dorothy asks Princess Ozma to bring Aunt Em and Uncle Henry to Oz, where Ozma gives them a permanent home and declares Dorothy a Princess of Oz. Wanting the older couple to have useful activity, Ozma sends them traveling with Dorothy, the Wizard, the Shaggy Man, and others. Their journey introduces them to many unusual places and peoples: the athletic college led by Professor H. M. Wogglebug, T.E.; the paper-doll Cuttenclips; the scattered Fuddles; Utensia’s living utensils; Bunbury’s edible inhabitants; Bunnybury’s rabbit kingdom; Rigmarole Town; and the fear-filled Flutterbudgets. Dorothy also helps the unhappy Rabbit King value his duty. During the journey, Ozma discovers through the Magic Picture that the Nome King’s tunnel is approaching the Emerald City. Dorothy’s companions, including the Tin Woodman, Scarecrow, and Jack Pumpkinhead, return to stand with Ozma. Although the invaders are immensely dangerous and Ozma refuses either to fight or flee, the Scarecrow devises a peaceful defense using the Forbidden Fountain’s Water of Oblivion. When the Nome King, Guph, the Nomes, and their treacherous allies emerge from the tunnel, they drink the water and forget who they are and why they came. Ozma sends the Nomes home under their king’s own forgotten orders, then uses the Magic Belt to return the remaining invaders safely to their lands. Finally, Glinda the Good protects Oz by making it invisible to all outsiders. In the closing message, Dorothy tells the writer that Oz is forever cut off from the rest of the world, and he wishes its people lasting happiness.

l: L. Frank Baum, The Emerald City of Oz
s: L. Frank Baum, formerly an author in his own conception, presents himself as an editor or private secretary for youngsters. He uses children’s ideas when possible and follows readers’ requests about Dorothy, Aunt Em, and Uncle Henry, seeking to please them.

l: children, The Emerald City of Oz
s: Children send L. Frank Baum clever ideas in letters; their imaginations and story suggestions help create his stories and inspire future fairy-tale authors.

l: readers, The Emerald City of Oz
s: Readers tell L. Frank Baum what to do with Dorothy, Aunt Em, and Uncle Henry, suggest future subjects, and are described by Baum as knowing what they want while he tries to please them.

l: the book, The Emerald City of Oz
s: is_attributed_to L. Frank Baum [on the title page] Baum suggests that the title page of the book might identify it as being by L. Frank Baum and his correspondents because children contributed many ideas to it.

l: children's ideas, The Emerald City of Oz
s: Children's ideas, conveyed to Baum in letters, are clever, logical, and interesting; he weaves them into his stories when possible.

l: Oz stories, The Emerald City of Oz
s: Oz stories are six books shaped partly by children’s ideas about Dorothy, Aunt Em, and Uncle Henry, offering useful, amusing lessons through quaint people and strange adventures, and ending with their story’s conclusion.

l: Dorothy, The Emerald City of Oz
s: Dorothy is a little girl from Kansas, raised and cared for by her beloved Aunt Em and Uncle Henry on a farm. She is usually loving and sweet-tempered, with a round rosy face and earnest eyes, and is described as simple, sweet, true, honest, and a dreamer. Though young, her adventures give her unusual experience and wisdom. She owns Toto, befriends Billina and many leading people of Oz, and is Ozma’s faithful friend and chosen companion. Her adventures in the Land of Oz make her important there: she captures the Nome King’s Magic Belt, destroys two wicked witches, finds the Scarecrow, and helps rescue Nick Chopper. Because the people love her and credit her with good luck, Ozma makes her a Princess of Oz, gives her rooms in the Emerald City palace, and brings Aunt Em and Uncle Henry from their threatened Kansas farm to live with her in Oz. Dorothy then travels through Oz with her relatives and companions, helping the Cuttenclips and Fuddles and learning the country’s people, customs, and places. When she becomes separated from the party, she is captured in Utensia with Toto and Billina but is released, then visits Bunbury and Bunnybury. In Bunnybury she becomes rabbit-sized, receives a royal welcome, and encourages the unhappy Rabbit King to consider the effect of his discontent on others. She returns safely to her companions and continues the journey. When the Nome King threatens Oz, Dorothy fears for Ozma, her friends, and her family. Although she considers using the Magic Belt to escape to Kansas, she refuses to abandon Oz and is willing to become a slave with its people. The danger ends when the invaders become harmless, and Glinda makes Oz invisible. Dorothy remains permanently in Oz with Aunt Em, Uncle Henry, and Toto, and says that she and Toto will always love the writer and the children who love them.

l: Aunt Em, The Emerald City of Oz
s: Aunt Em is Dorothy Gale’s aunt, Uncle Henry’s wife, and, with him, Dorothy’s guardian. An aging, feeble country woman and family housekeeper, she begins worried by poverty, the possible loss of the Kansas farm, and the prospect that Dorothy may need to work. Though heartbroken at possibly losing Dorothy, she accepts that Dorothy might be better off with her fairy friends. When Dorothy explains that Aunt Em and Uncle Henry are too old for hard work, Princess Ozma brings them to the Land of Oz and gives them a permanent palace home. Transported abruptly from housework in a calico dress and apron, Aunt Em is frightened and confused, then welcomed as an honored subject. Palace rooms, royal costumes, gold toilet articles, and leisure are more grandeur than she wants: she misses useful work and is troubled by having none. She nevertheless joins Dorothy’s travels, is impressed by Billina’s talking chicken family, and fiercely frightens the Lion with her gaze. She compares School Pills to medicine, doubts the value of matching the Fuddles, but helps find Lord High Chigglewitz’s pieces and shares the group’s amusement. She thinks the Love Magnet might have aided her Kansas family, dislikes the Rigmaroles’ excessive speech, and urges the travelers not to delay in Rigmarole Town. At the end, she is relieved by Dorothy’s return, though she thinks Dorothy is crazy for claiming to have eaten a wheelbarrow.

l: Uncle Henry, The Emerald City of Oz
s: Uncle Henry is Dorothy Gale's old, poor Kansas uncle, Aunt Em's husband, and, with her, Dorothy's guardian. A farmer whose mortgaged farm produces too little, he works as hard as he can but is too feeble and unhealthy to continue easily. After a cyclone destroys his house, he cannot repay the loan and faces losing his home. He doubts Dorothy's earlier adventures, taking them for dreams, and worries that she may be mistreated in the fairyland she describes. Ozma brings him from his barn to the Emerald City's Throne Room, ending his financial danger and offering him a permanent palace home in Oz, where he need not work unless he wishes. Startled at first, he accepts the palace and Munchkin-style clothes, selects a blue satin suit, and independently dresses himself. He explores with Aunt Em, recognizes Dorothy's friend the Cowardly Lion, and later finds Oz preferable to Kansas. Yet idleness makes him restless; feeding chickens and joining Dorothy's journey give him activity. On that journey he marvels at the speaking Sawhorse, offers practical suggestions about the Fuddles, helps match Lord High Chigglewitz, welcomes Dorothy back, and criticizes needless delay in Rigmarole Town. He later travels with the Wizard, has traveled to California and Australia, and becomes Keeper of the Jewels in the Royal Storehouses.

l: the alliance between Baum and children, The Emerald City of Oz
s: Baum's continuing alliance with children is shaped by their ideas and his wish to please them, and he hopes it lasts a long time.

l: Nome King, The Emerald City of Oz
s: Nome King, also called Roquat the Red and Roquat, is the powerful but persistently angry, very bad king and tyrant of the Nomes and Nome Kingdom. His central motive is revenge against Dorothy, Ozma, and Oz after the loss of his Magic Belt, his defeat, and the liberation of his slaves. Although the belt is described as his rightful possession and as King Roquat's Magic Belt, Dorothy and her companions later steal it, greatly reducing his power. He resolves to recover it through conquest. Roquat plans to invade Oz, destroy the Emerald City, enslave its people, capture Ozma and Dorothy, and turn them into china ornaments. After angrily discarding advisers who frustrate him, he appoints General Guph, orders miners and Nomes to dig a broad tunnel under the deadly desert, and personally inspects and hastens the work. He bargains with evil spirits and gathers the Whimsies, Growleywogs, and Phanfasms, though he fears the Phanfasms may conquer the Nomes and the Growleywogs secretly intend to enslave him after Oz falls. The tunnel reaches beneath Ozma's palace grounds. Roquat leads fifty thousand armed Nomes with Guph in an invasion intended to seize the Magic Belt, dismiss his allies afterward, and let the Nomes ravage Oz. At the invasion, however, the Scarecrow and Tin Woodman throw him into the Forbidden Fountain. He forgets everything, and Ozma persuades him to order the Nomes to march home, ending his planned vengeance and conquest.

l: Ozma, The Emerald City of Oz
s: Ozma is the beautiful, beloved fairy-powered Princess and ruler of the Land of Oz, living in the Emerald City palace and governing all its countries. Her magical resources include a fairy wand, the Magic Belt, and the Magic Picture; she also has the Cowardly Lion and Hungry Tiger as bodyguards and favors the Sawhorse as a steed. What matters most is her compassionate, just care for Oz and its people: she attends to their welfare, settles disputes fairly, welcomes and houses Uncle Henry and Aunt Em, gives Dorothy her rightful rank as Princess of Oz, and supports Dorothy's journeys and requests. Ozma's rule faces danger from Roquat the Red and the Nomes, who seek to destroy or enslave her and conquer Oz. Although she had previously led a conquest against the Nomes after they enslaved the Royal Family of Ev, she learns through the Magic Picture that Roquat has built a tunnel into Oz and refuses military resistance, believing Oz cannot defeat the invaders. She will neither abandon her people nor save herself while they are enslaved, choosing instead to share their fate and meet the attackers peacefully at the Forbidden Fountain. There she identifies the amnesiac Nome King as Roquat, persuades him to send his army home, and uses the Magic Belt to return the other invaders to their homes. Concerned that future outsiders may enter by tunnels or other routes, she seeks Glinda's help and agrees to make Oz invisible, separating it from the outside world for protection.

l: Nomes, The Emerald City of Oz
s: The Nomes are immortal underground beings and subjects of Roquat, the Nome King, living in his extensive caverns. They are miners and metal workers when not serving as soldiers, with great muscular strength gained through forging and mining, rock-colored uniforms, and skill in tunnel construction. Though good fighters, they are weak in magic and are judged not strong enough to conquer the Emerald City without help. Under Guph's command, they drill a long tunnel through solid rock beneath the Deadly Desert toward Oz, preparing an Invincible Army to march on the Emerald City for conquest, plunder, and slaves. They seek aid from the Whimsies and Growleywogs; the Growleywogs agree but secretly plan to conquer the Nomes afterward. The Nomes have previously been defeated by Oz people and remain vulnerable to hen's eggs, which are poisonous to underground beings. Guph therefore intends to keep them behind other forces, and they would flee from Billina's eggs. They remain allied with their underground monarch in the planned conquest and destruction of Oz.

l: the Nome King's army, The Emerald City of Oz
s: The Nome King's army is a force of fifty thousand well-drilled Nome soldiers, armed with swords and pikes, wearing rock-colored uniforms, and belonging to and commanded by King Roquat the Red. General Blug first warns that it cannot cross the deadly desert and cannot withstand Princess Ozma's fairy powers. Roquat instead plans a tunnel route. General Guph leads the army for a surprise emergence in the Emerald City and a conquest of Oz alongside the Whimsies, Growleywogs, and Phanfasms, although the Phanfasms secretly intend to destroy it afterward.

l: the Land of Oz, The Emerald City of Oz
s: The Land of Oz is a mighty, beautiful, peaceful fairy country and fairyland beyond the Deadly Desert, ordinarily unreachable by crossing it. Ruled by Ozma, it has the Emerald City as its capital, a palace, happy and contented people, great riches, unusual people and places, and beautiful weather. Its country includes the Country of the Winkies, Utensia, Bunbury, Bunnybury, and Rigmarole Town. It has no recorded starvation; people may eat surplus eggs but do not eat chickens. Dorothy, Billina, and Toto are non-fairies in Oz, and Dorothy is especially beloved for the good she has done. Oz becomes the permanent, safe, and delightful home of Dorothy, Uncle Henry, and Aunt Em, who are welcomed with respect and told they belong there. The central development is a threat to this protected country.
